## Executive assessment

Canva's breach is especially useful as a study of how a technically qualified explanation can produce an overly reassuring message. The historical record distinguishes access to protected password records from recovery of usable passwords, and both from unauthorized entry into a user's account. Those distinctions should guide the response, but they should not obscure the action a user needs to take.

This account is deliberately shorter than some other TeamStarWolf studies. Most detailed first-party incident evidence is concentrated in one evolving company FAQ. The article adds independently maintained breach records, institutional advisories and original password-security research, without stretching that limited forensic record into a fictional attack narrative. Its main contribution is an evidence comparison and an editorial audit of how to communicate residual risk.

## 1. Compact company chronology

Canva reported interrupting an attack on May 24, 2019. Its June update described exposure of up to 139 million profiles and bcrypt-protected passwords for password logins. It distinguished an attacker claim about OAuth tokens from its own lack of evidence of token download or key access. It reported viewing of limited historical payment information, without evidence of theft, and no indication of access to designs. Active pre-breach login tokens were reset. [1]

The August update acknowledged surprise among some recipients of external alerts. It explained hashing while opening its password reassurance categorically. On January 11, 2020, Canva learned of approximately four million accounts with recovered passwords. It reset unchanged historical passwords on January 12 and described the response in a January 17 update. These are stages of one historical incident, not evidence of a new January intrusion. [1]

The sequence raises an incident-specific question: when a provider knows that verification records have escaped its control, how long should an unchanged secret remain usable? A difficult-to-recover password can still be a potentially exposed password. The timing of forced action and the wording of earlier recommendations should therefore be evaluated together rather than as unrelated communications choices.

## 2. The count is not a single interchangeable number

Have I Been Pwned describes the Canva collection as affecting about 137 million subscribers and displays 137.3 million affected addresses. It lists email addresses, names, usernames, geographic information and bcrypt password hashes for users without social logins. It records addition to its service on August 9, 2019. These are HIBP's collection descriptors and publication timing, not an independent count of completed account takeovers. [2]

The difference from the company's upper-bound profile figure should remain visible. The sources use different labels and levels of precision. Without a reconciliation, a writer should not assume that the difference represents recovered accounts, an initial exaggeration, a deduplication operation or records the attacker failed to steal. Each is a possible explanation that would require evidence; none is established merely by subtracting the figures.

Likewise, a recovered-password population is not the same as the total profile population. A social-login account may be represented in profile information without having the same kind of password record. A person can have multiple addresses, and an address appearing in a breach record does not demonstrate that its mailbox was entered. Keeping the unit attached to each figure prevents the headline from quietly changing meaning across an article or slide deck.

## 3. Hashing and recovery: the technical distinction

The original bcrypt research explains password verification through one-way functions and proposes an adaptable computational cost. A password can be tested against a stored verifier without treating that verifier as ordinary reversible ciphertext. The purpose of added cost is to make guessing more expensive; it does not create a guarantee that every user-selected secret will resist recovery. [3]

That distinction changes the language appropriate to a historical breach. Describing a password as decrypted can imply that an attacker obtained an encryption key or broke an encryption algorithm. In an account involving password hashes, recovered or cracked may be more precise unless the evidence establishes a different mechanism. The study does not claim that Canva's underlying algorithm was cryptographically broken, and it does not infer the attacker's hardware, cost parameter, guessing strategy or exact work rate.

The relevant lesson is limited but important: protection at rest reduces some consequences of unauthorized retrieval without making retrieval harmless. A live service can restrict online attempts, while a copied verifier is no longer controlled by that service's login interface. This is conceptual explanation, not an operational cracking procedure. No stolen collection was acquired or tested for this research.

## 4. How external alerts changed the audience

Mozilla Monitor records the breach date as May 24, 2019 and database addition as August 9, 2019, and states that its breach information comes from HIBP. Mozilla and HIBP therefore should not be counted as two independent forensic confirmations of the collection. Mozilla's record is valuable as evidence of a separate delivery channel with an explicitly named upstream source. [4]

This is a distinctive feature of the incident's communication history. A person can first learn of an old event through a monitoring service, even if the provider previously sent a message. The later alert does not establish a later intrusion. It does establish another opportunity, and another burden, to explain what the dates mean and what action remains necessary.

An incident archive should preserve the difference between sending a notice and achieving understanding. Delivery to an old address, a message overlooked among ordinary marketing, or a user who believes a technical reassurance removes urgency can all lead to incomplete action. Those are possible failure modes, not findings about every Canva user. The reviewed record does not supply a complete notification-delivery or password-change funnel, so this article does not invent one.

## 5. Institutional response beyond the design platform

The University of the Philippines IT Development Center issued a Canva advisory on August 13, 2019. It directed UP Mail users to the company's incident material and HIBP, recommended password changes for affected accounts and reminded users about two-step verification details. This is primary evidence of the university's own communication, not an independent reconstruction of the attack. [5]

Miami University published a further advisory on February 28, 2020. It identified students and faculty among affected Canva users, addressed reused institutional passwords and explained how to respond to an unexpected Duo prompt. The page's current maintenance timestamp is later than its publication date; this study uses the original publication date for the response chronology. [6]

These two advisories show how a consumer or creative-service breach can become an institutional identity concern. Neither notice proves that either university's own infrastructure was breached through Canva. The risk pathway is the potential reuse of a secret or the targeting of someone identified through an exposed address. A university's protective message should not be misreported as evidence of a successful secondary compromise.

The distinction also explains why a provider's reset cannot finish every user's recovery. A service can invalidate a secret within its own system, but it cannot ordinarily replace the same secret at an unrelated employer, school or mailbox provider. The institutional advisories address that boundary. Their value lies in making a specific action relevant to their audiences, rather than merely repeating a global breach headline.

## 6. What behavioral research can and cannot add

Bhagavatula, Bauer and Kapadia studied password changes using data from 249 participants, collected during 2017-2018. Their results found limited constructive response to breaches and incomplete changes to similar passwords on other services. This is contextual research about observed behavior. Its sample predates the Canva incident and must not be presented as a measurement of Canva users. [7]

The study supports testing the assumption that a recommendation automatically produces the desired action. It does not establish how many Canva users ignored a warning or why a particular person retained a password. There is a major difference between using research to frame an evaluation question and importing its percentage into a victim company's population.

For this case, the useful evaluation question is whether the response reduced the number of still-valid historical secrets and whether people understood the separate risk of reuse. A campaign's message count, a partnership offer or a page-view total would not answer that question on its own. The public record reviewed here lacks the data needed to compute a completion rate, and that limitation should be preserved.

## 7. Exact editorial improvements for a case-study audit

The following are original proposed edits for the TeamStarWolf account, not quotations from Canva and not claims that Canva used the replacement wording.

**Replace broad password reassurance with:** "The attacker obtained protected password records. The protection makes recovery harder but does not remove the need to change an affected, unchanged password."

This keeps the protective value of hashing while making the required action visible. A reader should not need to reconcile an initially reassuring sentence with a later caution buried in a technical explanation.

**Replace an unexplained count with:** "The company reported an upper-bound profile population; HIBP reports affected addresses in the collection it processed. These figures are not directly interchangeable."

This prevents a single number from drifting among profiles, subscribers, passwords and people. If a later source reconciles the figures, the article can add that explanation without rewriting the earlier statements as if they never differed.

**Replace a universal no-impact statement with:** "The investigation reported no evidence of the specific activity described, as of that update."

The proposed wording preserves the object and time of a negative finding. It avoids turning lack of evidence of one kind of access into a guarantee about every possible consequence.

**Replace a new-breach implication in a later update with:** "New evidence about old stolen data triggered another protective action."

This helps users understand why an incident can require attention again without implying that a separate intrusion occurred. It also keeps the original exposure and the later response on one coherent timeline.

**Replace a claim of proof from a reset with:** "The reset is a precaution; whether an account was entered requires separate evidence."

Protective action can be justified before misuse is demonstrated. The audit should not force a choice between acting cautiously and describing the evidence accurately.

## 8. Remaining investigative gaps and conclusion

The reviewed sources do not establish the exact entry vector, a full sequence of attacker movements, a verified real-world identity, a reconciled account-level extraction total or a complete financial-loss figure. The company FAQ refers to a future technical postmortem, but this research pass did not locate a separate detailed public report. That is a search limitation, not proof that no internal report or later publication exists.

This case should consequently be taught as a documented exposure-and-response history with a strong communication lesson, rather than as a fully reconstructed intrusion. The most defensible recommendations concern the connection between known exposure, residual uncertainty and required action. A statement about a protective technology should clarify the risk decision, not replace it.

The broader lesson is that historical authentication data can remain consequential after the initial containment. A case study becomes more useful when it tracks changes in evidence and response while resisting unsupported claims about attribution, cryptographic failure or universal harm. Here, a shorter, source-bounded account is more reliable than adding a generic security checklist to reach an arbitrary length.

## Source register

[1] Canva, evolving May 24 incident FAQ with June and August 2019 and January 2020 updates. Company account, read in full for incident sections. https://www.canva.com/help/incident-may24/

[2] Have I Been Pwned, Canva breach record. Collection descriptors and affected-address count, not a confirmed takeover count. https://haveibeenpwned.com/Breach/Canva/

[3] Niels Provos and David Mazieres, A Future-Adaptable Password Scheme, introduction, USENIX 1999. Historical mechanism context, not Canva implementation evidence. https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/usenix99/provos/provos_html/node1.html

[4] Mozilla Monitor, Canva record. Explicitly dependent on HIBP data. https://monitor.mozilla.org/en/breach-details/Canva

[5] University of the Philippines IT Development Center, 13 August 2019 advisory. Primary institutional response record. https://itdc.up.edu.ph/about/advisories/2019%2008%2013%20SECURITY%20ADVISORY%20for%20Canva%20Users%20-%20Review%20Your%20Email%20Security.pdf

[6] Miami University IT Services, published 28 February 2020 advisory. Primary institutional response; later maintenance timestamp distinguished. https://miamioh.edu/it-services/news-media/2020/02/canva-breach.html

[7] Bhagavatula, Bauer and Kapadia, (How) Do people change their passwords after a breach?, 2020. Abstract, introduction and methodology inspected; pre-Canva sample, contextual only. https://arxiv.org/html/2010.09853v1
